standard.title: Develop a Response to an Economic Issue
standard.description: develop a response to an economic and business issue, identifying potential costs and benefits
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can develop evidence-based conclusions and propose actions with assessed effects (AC9HS6S05, AC9HS6S06). The Year 7 demand adds the economic frame of costs and benefits — structuring a response to an issue by explicitly identifying and weighing the trade-offs involved, and explaining that a decision selects one alternative over another.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop a response to an economic and business issue, identifying potential costs and benefits.

nodes.label: What counts as a cost and a benefit
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the potential costs and benefits of an economic decision, recognising that both financial and non-financial factors count.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one cost and one benefit for a given decision; include at least one non-financial factor.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the potential costs and benefits of an economic decision — including both financial and non-financial factors such as time, opportunity cost, social impact; distinguish direct from indirect costs and benefits; apply to realistic consumer and community decisions.
wider: Analyse costs and benefits in a government resource allocation decision — where community benefit may be broad and indirect, and costs distributed unevenly across groups
Examine how a First Nations community might assess the costs and benefits of a new economic development proposal — weighing financial returns against cultural, environmental and community impacts
Evaluate a historical business decision by identifying costs and benefits at the time versus in retrospect — exploring how uncertainty affects cost-benefit analysis
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who reduce costs and benefits to financial amounts only will be unable to construct a complete response to an economic issue. Non-financial costs and benefits — time, social impact, opportunity cost, environmental effects — are essential to the full economic analysis demanded by the descriptor and the integration node.

response_modes.reason: The cost-benefit scaffold needs to be explicit: costs = what you give up (money, time, other options); benefits = what you gain (money, time, satisfaction, community good). Students need the non-financial categories named and modelled before applying independently.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one financial and one non-financial cost and benefit for a given decision
Explains why each factor counts as a cost or benefit

nodes.label: Reasoning from cost-benefit to a response
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can combine known knowledge with new ideas to develop a response to an economic issue, using costs and benefits to justify the response.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a response to a structured issue — such as a purchase or part-time work decision — that uses identified costs and benefits as the reasoning basis.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a response to an issue by combining known knowledge with new ideas — for example, using a product statement and personal budget to identify benefits and costs of a mobile phone purchase; explain why making an economic decision involves selecting one alternative over another; use cost-benefit reasoning as the explicit justification structure.
wider: Develop a response to a community-level economic issue (e.g. 'Should the local council convert parkland to commercial development?') using a full cost-benefit analysis
Develop a response that explicitly addresses a sustainability dimension — identifying costs that accrue over time or benefits that are only realised in the long term
Develop a response to an economic issue facing a First Nations community, engaging with the specific costs and benefits as understood from within that community context

response_modes.reason: Students need practice constructing the full reasoning chain: 'The issue is X. The alternatives are A and B. The costs of A are... the benefits of A are... Therefore my response is A, because...' Without this scaffold, cost-benefit identification stays at listing rather than becoming the basis of a reasoned response.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of decision contexts — personal purchases, community resource allocation, business decisions, First Nations development choices — all warrant genuine cost-benefit analysis but with meaningfully different structures and stakeholders. Wider engagement with this range builds transferable economic reasoning.
success_criteria: Develops a response to an economic issue that identifies costs and benefits of the chosen option
Explains why one alternative was selected over another using cost-benefit reasoning
